_doc: The adapter's map for one project: <root>/systems/godot.json. adapters/godot_tables.py reads it and writes systems/tables/*.csv from the Godot project's .tres files and script defaults; export.py reads it back to check or write the tables into the engine. Copy this template and rename what the project calls things; a project on another engine writes another adapter to the same tables.
game: the Godot project folder, relative to the root (holds project.godot).

constants: one row of constants.csv per entry. key is the skill's word for the number (rules.py and sim.py read these names; keep them). from is `<script_class>#<property>` for an exported property of the one resource of that class, or `<path to a .gd>#<property>` for a script's export default (a number the project keeps on a node, like the ammo pool's base). doc is what the number means, written into the table.

tables: per csv, the resources that are its rows. classes: the script_class values that belong to it (two weapon classes make one weapons table). id: the property that names the row. columns: property -> column; a column named after the property is written `"power": "power"`; a constant per class goes in `by_class` (kind melee/ranged from the class). sub: the property holding an Array of sub-resources when the rows live inside one resource (a shop's entries); then every sub-resource is a row and the file is one.

enemies: the stats table the enemy-designer reads, enemies/stats.csv, refreshed from the EnemyConfig resources; columns map csv column -> property. Columns not listed (met_at_level, placed) are kept as they are; a row with no resource is kept and reported. name_from strips the resource file name to the row name (elite_scav.tres -> elite_scav).
player: where the skill reads the player's timings it does not own: the enemy-designer's enemies/player.json (reaction time, the dash, the i-frames). Keep unless the project keeps them elsewhere.

enums: per table, a column whose engine value is an enum int, with the names in enum order; the adapter writes the name into the csv and export.py writes the int back. district: the level-designer's district.json when the project has one; sim.py reads the specs' door-level gates through it (without it the room list's per-room requires gate entry, which is coarser).

starting: on a table, `<class>#<array property>` naming the resources the player owns from the start (an item catalog's starting_items); the table gets a `starting` column. A hack's ownership flag is a column (`flag`): empty means owned from the start, otherwise the kit id after the last dot must be granted by a room.
